title: La familia
goal: Talk about your family: who they are, their ages and what they're like, with tener and my / your / his / our.

lessons.title: My family
lessons.notes:
Family words come in pairs: **-o** for the man, **-a** for the woman - **el hermano** (brother), **la hermana** (sister); **el hijo** (son), **la hija** (daughter).
The masculine plural covers a mixed group, which is very handy:
**los hermanos** = brothers, or brothers and sisters (siblings)
**los hijos** = sons, or children
**los padres** = fathers, or (usually) parents
So **Tengo dos hermanos** can mean two brothers, or a brother and a sister. **El bebé** is masculine even for a baby girl.

accept_en: I have a brother and a sister.

sentences.en: My wife is in the house.

lessons.title: Grandparents, cousins and tener
lessons.notes:
The whole of **tener** (to have):
**yo** tengo · **tú** tienes · **él / ella / usted** tiene · **nosotros** tenemos · **ellos / ustedes** tienen
(Spain: vosotros **tenéis**.)
Notice the e in the stem becomes **ie** in most forms - you'll meet this 'boot' pattern again in unit 15.
Older and younger brothers or sisters: **el hermano mayor** (older brother), **la hermana menor** (younger sister). Mayor and menor don't change for gender.
**El novio / la novia** is a boyfriend / girlfriend, and also a groom / bride.

sentences.es: Tengo un hermano mayor y una hermana menor.
sentences.en: I have an older brother and a younger sister.
accept_en: I've got an older brother and a younger sister.

sentences.es: Ellos tienen un perro y un gato.

My grandma is a lot of fun.

Los abuelos de Ana son de Colombia.

accept_en: My cousin is twenty years old.

lessons.title: My, your, his, our
lessons.notes:
Possessives match the **thing owned**, not the owner:
**mi** casa → **mis** casas (my) · **tu** hermano → **tus** hermanos (your)
**su** casa → **sus** casas (his, her, its, their, your-formal)
**nuestro** hijo, **nuestra** hija, **nuestros** hijos, **nuestras** hijas (our)
So 'our house' is **nuestra casa** even if two men own it - casa is feminine.
**Su** has many owners; if it's unclear, say **la casa de Ana** (Ana's house). Spain also has vuestro / vuestra (your, of vosotros).

accept_en: Where are your brothers and sisters?

sentences.es: Nuestra casa está cerca de la playa.
sentences.en: Our house is near the beach.
accept_en: Our house is close to the beach.

sentences.es: Tus llaves están en la mesa.
sentences.en: Your keys are on the table.

lessons.title: Talking about your family
lessons.notes:
Being married or single: Latin Americans usually say **estoy casado / casada** (I'm married), seeing it as a state; **soy casado** is heard too, and both are fine. The same goes for **soltero** (single) and **divorciado**.
An only child is **hijo único** or **hija única**: **Soy hija única** - no 'un' or 'una', just like jobs.
**¿Cómo se llama?** asks what someone's (or a pet's) name is: **¿Cómo se llama tu perro?** - **Se llama Max.**
**Juntos / juntas** = together, and it matches the group.
